title: Backpacker with sudden fever, aches and nausea on day 10

classification.acuity_basis: No evacuation criteria met; persistent symptoms and upcoming high pass prompted supported walk-out.

presentation.summary: Day 10 of a trip, a participant has had sudden headache, nausea, muscle aches, fever, chills and low energy for 24 hours. No one else is sick.
presentation.last_intake_output: 3 L yesterday, little food, clear urine

assessment: flu-like illness; no evacuation trigger yet
plan: boil utensils, group handwashing to limit spread
teaching_points: Flu-like and GI illness are ~40% of NOLS illness incidents; most spread by hands.
Flu-like symptoms can mask pneumonia, PE, or MI.

Evacuate for: fever >48 h or >39C; stiff neck, severe headache, breathing difficulty or wheeze; pneumonia signs; GI pain >12 h, bloody diarrhea, dehydration; can't keep fluids >48 h; sore throat unable to swallow or with fever and white patches; sudden severe headache or altered mental status.
Care: rest, fluids, hygiene, analgesic/antipyretic, bland diet.

decision_points.question: Evacuate?
decision_points.source_decision: Day 2: walk out supported, without pack

outcome.summary: Developed productive cough by next day; walked out supported by group. Final diagnosis not given.

must_ask: how high is the fever and for how long?
trouble breathing or coughing up phlegm?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if fever >39C or >48 h, stiff neck, breathing difficulty, or altered mental status.
must_not_recommend: crossing a high pass while ill without reassessment

friend got sick with chills and nausea in the backcountry

title: Sea kayaker with cramps and a positive heel-tap sign: ruptured appendix

source.title: Case Study 19: Stomach Cramps on a Kayaking Trip

classification.acuity_basis: Severe pain episode and peritoneal sign met evacuation criteria; helicopter; ruptured appendix.

context.distance_to_care: paddle to town/hatchery; Coast Guard helicopter

presentation.summary: Two days of feeling poorly with occasional diarrhea, then 30 minutes of 10/10 cramping pain overnight with a board-hard belly. Now 2/10 dull generalized pain. Declines full exam.
presentation.chief_complaint: don't feel great but I've felt worse
exam_findings: sharp RLQ pain with right heel tap (peritoneal sign)
presentation.last_intake_output: hydrated, clear urine, light breakfast, no BM today

assessment: possible appendicitis or other serious abdominal problem
teaching_points: Use OPQRST to characterize abdominal pain.
Focus on evacuation triggers, not diagnosis.

Evacuate abdominal pain >12 h; localized pain with guarding, rigidity, distension; peritoneal signs (pain with jarring/heel tap); shock signs; blood in vomit/stool/urine; prolonged N/V/D; fever >39C; possible pregnancy.
Patients who minimize symptoms can delay critical care.

outcome.summary: Patient refused radio; paddled toward town, pain worsened, vomited; Coast Guard helicopter from fish hatchery. Ruptured appendix with serious infection; full recovery after long stay.

must_recognize: pain improvement after severe episode can mean rupture
must_ask: does it hurt when you jump, walk, or hit a bump?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate abdominal pain >12 h or with peritoneal signs.
must_not_recommend: waiting it out because pain improved

lay_queries: really bad stomach cramps last night and now it's a dull ache
belly hurts when I bump it on the kayak

title: Ranch biologist with spiking fever two days after a tick bite

source.title: Case Study: Treating a Feverish Patient

classification.acuity_basis: Fever to 40C after tick bite meets evacuation threshold; clinic overnight.

context.weather: early May, fine; heavy tick season (Dermacentor)
context.distance_to_care: clinic ~2 h by dirt road; satellite phone

presentation.summary: Colleague has 24 hours of headache, nausea, aches, fever and chills. A tick was found embedded in his armpit two days ago. Temperature swings between 38 and 40C over the morning.
presentation.chief_complaint: feels unwell, aches and nausea, worse overnight
presentation.last_intake_output: 3 L yesterday, little food, clear urine
presentation.events_leading_up: embedded tick removed from left axilla 2 days ago

assessment: flu-like illness with high fever at evacuation threshold
plan: call clinic by satellite phone when it opens
teaching_points: Tick-borne diseases include spotted fever, tick fever, relapsing fever, tularemia, babesiosis, Lyme.
Check body for ticks at least twice daily; permethrin-treated clothing.
Remove with tweezers close to skin, steady pull, wash site; no heat, nail polish, or alcohol.
Tick bite plus fever, rash, flu-like symptoms or myalgia needs physician evaluation.
Evacuate fever >48 h, >39C, or with severe headache or stiff neck.

outcome.summary: Driven to clinic; overnight stay; probable tick fever; ill ~1 week, weak another, then returned.

must_recognize: fever after tick bite needs medical evaluation
must_ask: any tick bites in the last few weeks?
eval.must_escalate: See a physician for fever after tick exposure; evacuate if >39C.
must_not_recommend: dismissing as flu without asking about ticks

lay_queries: I had a tick bite and now I have a high fever
how do I remove a tick
fever and aches after being in tick country

title: Known epileptic has a generalized seizure in camp

classification.acuity_basis: Single seizure, full recovery to A+Ox4; walked out per protocol for physician evaluation.

pertinent_history: seizure disorder after head injury 6 years ago; seizure-free 1 year

presentation.summary: After a 4-mile hike a participant rolls out of a camp chair and has a ~45-second generalized seizure with incontinence. Leader removes a spoon from his mouth; he remains unresponsive with noisy breathing that clears after wiping saliva.
exam_findings: noisy breathing improved with clearing saliva

plan: protect airway in postictal period, recovery position
walk to trailhead and evacuate for physician evaluation
anticipated_problems: failure to wake or repeat seizures -> rapid evacuation
teaching_points: Seizure care is protective: move hazards, cushion head, don't restrain.
Never force the mouth open or insert anything; people don't swallow their tongue.
After: open airway, recovery position, check injuries; postictal confusion may last 10+ min.
Serious: repeated seizures without waking between, or seizure from diabetes or head injury -> rapid evacuation.
Isolated seizure in known epileptic: physician evaluation but not necessarily rapid evacuation; check for missed doses.

outcome.summary: Rested, ate, hiked to trailhead by 21:00; physician cleared for home but not field.

must_ask: how long did the seizure last?
has he had seizures before? taken his medicine?
eval.must_escalate: Call for rapid evacuation if seizure >5 min, repeated seizures, no recovery, injury, diabetes, or first-ever seizure.
must_not_recommend: giving food or drink before fully awake

lay_queries: my friend is having a seizure what do I do
he was shaking all over and now won't wake up
someone had a fit and bit their tongue

classification.acuity_basis: Resolved with 20 min of breathing coaching; no evacuation.

pertinent_history: says he 'may have asthma', never used inhaler

presentation.summary: Fifteen feet below the edge on rappel, an anxious student freezes, clenching the brake. Once lowered he is dizzy, says he can't breathe, with numb painful hands and tingling lips.

plan: move to shade out of wind
teaching_points: Hyperventilation lowers CO2: tingling, hand/foot spasm, sometimes chest pain, sense of suffocation.
Treat by calming and coaching slow breaths; may take time.
Paper-bag rebreathing is no longer recommended.
No wheeze or allergic signs makes asthma unlikely.
Don't give someone else's inhaler without indication.

outcome.summary: RR 12 after ~20 min coaching; spasms resolved; rested rest of afternoon.

must_ask: history of asthma or panic attacks?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if wheeze, chest pain, or no resolution.
must_not_recommend: using another person's inhaler without wheeze

lay_queries: he's panicking and says he can't breathe and his hands are tingling
breathing really fast and lips are numb

title: Teen with 22 hours of worsening lower abdominal pain 12 miles from a road

source.title: Case Study 4: Abdominal Pain on the Trail

classification.acuity_basis: Pain >12 h, worse with jarring: meets evacuation protocol; helicopter requested.

presentation.summary: A teen moaned all night with lower belly pain that began as a cramp yesterday morning and is now sharp, 8/10, worse with walking downhill or hopping. Nauseated.
presentation.last_intake_output: little dinner, 1 cup water this AM, clear urine, no BM today

assessment: acute abdominal pain meeting evacuation protocol (>12 h, worse with movement/jarring)
plan: request helicopter evacuation via program base
if no signal, team of four hikes out to call
clear fluids only if tolerated and evacuation delayed, otherwise nothing by mouth
teaching_points: ~27% of NOLS illness is GI; ~7% acute abdominal pain.
Gastroenteritis: intermittent diffuse cramps, vomiting/diarrhea, low fever.
Appendicitis classically dull periumbilical pain moving to RLQ with nausea and anorexia; often atypical.
Look for evacuation triggers rather than a diagnosis.

must_recognize: abdominal pain >12 h with jarring pain = evacuate
must_ask: does walking or hopping make it worse?
must_not_recommend: hiking him out with full pack

lay_queries: kid's stomach has hurt all night and walking makes it worse
sharp lower belly pain while backpacking

title: 49-year-old with racing heart and hyperventilation on a corporate rappel

source.title: Case Study: Anxiety or Cardiac Episode?

classification.acuity_basis: Cardiac cause could not be excluded in a 49-year-old with palpitations; EMS called.

context.distance_to_care: off-road vehicle to ambulance at paved lot

presentation.summary: Reluctant, height-fearful participant stops 15 ft below a cliff lip looking very unwell, gripping the ropes. Lowered to ground he is pacing, dizzy, 'wired', with pounding heart, nausea, tingling hands and lips.

plan: evacuate via EMS because cardiac cause cannot be ruled out
teaching_points: Don't let an emotional presentation hide a physical problem.
Stress reactions that resolve can stay in the field; persistent or unpredictable ones usually need evacuation.
Evacuate chest pain that isn't clearly musculoskeletal.
Cardiac events don't always cause classic chest pain; be conservative.

outcome.summary: EMS transported to hospital; rejoined group that evening feeling better. Diagnosis not stated.

must_ask: any chest pain, pressure, or pain in arm/jaw?
eval.must_escalate: Call EMS if cardiac cause can't be excluded.
must_not_recommend: dismissing as just anxiety in an older adult with palpitations

lay_queries: my coworker's heart is racing and he can't breathe after the rappel
is this a panic attack or a heart attack
